clinicalPearls: Effective acute pain control improves comfort, supports early mobilisation and recovery, and reduces complications such as respiratory compromise and the risk of persistent postsurgical pain

A multimodal approach combines analgesics with different mechanisms (paracetamol, anti-inflammatories, regional or neuraxial techniques, and opioids when needed) to improve relief while limiting side effects
Opioid-sparing strategies reduce nausea, sedation, ileus, and respiratory depression, and are central to enhanced recovery pathways
Regular assessment using pain scores at rest and on movement guides titration, and analgesia should be tailored to the individual and the surgical procedure
Regional and neuraxial techniques provide excellent targeted analgesia but require monitoring for block-related complications and, with neuraxial opioids, delayed respiratory depression
Opioid therapy demands vigilance for oversedation and respiratory depression, particularly in the elderly, those with sleep apnoea, and when combined with other sedatives
Special populations, including opioid-tolerant patients, those with substance use disorders, children, and the elderly, need individualised plans and often specialist input
Poorly controlled acute pain is a risk factor for developing chronic postsurgical pain, so proactive, adequate management has longer-term benefits
reference.pathophysiology: Acute pain after surgery or injury arises from tissue damage that activates peripheral nociceptors and releases inflammatory mediators, sensitising both peripheral nerves and central pathways. Nociceptive signals travel via the dorsal horn to higher centres, where they are modulated by descending inhibitory and facilitatory systems. Peripheral and central sensitisation lower pain thresholds and amplify responses, contributing to hyperalgesia. Because pain is transmitted and modulated at multiple sites, combining agents that act at different points in these pathways (peripheral inflammation, nerve conduction, spinal transmission, and central perception) produces additive or synergistic relief with fewer dose-related adverse effects.
additionalDifferentials: Pain from a surgical complication such as bleeding, ischaemia, or infection
Compartment syndrome presenting as disproportionate pain
Referred pain from another organ system
Anxiety or distress amplifying pain report
Undiagnosed acute cardiac or abdominal event
additionalInvestigations: Regular pain scoring at rest and on movement
Assessment for sedation and respiratory rate when opioids are used
Evaluation for a surgical or vascular cause when pain is severe or escalating
Assessment for compartment syndrome when pain is disproportionate
Review of the analgesic regimen and its effectiveness and side effects
redFlags: Pain that is severe, escalating, or disproportionate, suggesting compartment syndrome or a surgical complication
Excessive sedation or a falling respiratory rate indicating opioid-induced respiratory depression
New neurological deficit after neuraxial or regional analgesia
Pain accompanied by signs of ischaemia, sepsis, or haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Most acute pain resolves as healing progresses, and good multimodal control aids recovery; inadequate management increases complications and the likelihood of chronic postsurgical pain.
pitfalls: Relying on opioids alone rather than a multimodal, opioid-sparing plan
Missing compartment syndrome or a surgical complication behind disproportionate pain
Underestimating opioid respiratory-depression risk in vulnerable patients
Failing to reassess and titrate analgesia to individual response
Neglecting the special needs of opioid-tolerant patients and those with substance use disorders
management: Multimodal analgesia combining paracetamol and anti-inflammatories as the foundation
Regional and neuraxial techniques for targeted analgesia within opioid-sparing enhanced-recovery pathways
Opioids reserved for moderate-to-severe or breakthrough pain, titrated to effect
Adjuncts such as ketamine, gabapentinoids, or local anaesthetic infiltration for refractory or neuropathic pain
Regular pain assessment at rest and on movement to guide titration and tailor analgesia to the procedure
Vigilant monitoring for oversedation and respiratory depression, especially in the elderly, those with sleep apnoea, or on other sedatives
Referral to the acute pain service for complex or poorly controlled pain
